fact: MacTutor gives Pythagoras as born about 570 BC and dead about 490 BC, so a floruit near -530 is consistent; the record already marks the attribution of the ratios to him as legend-level.
note: Read MacTutor's Pythagoras page for his dates; no text by Pythagoras exists, so the attribution itself cannot be settled and stays a low-confidence precursor.

fact: Wikipedia's claim that Wylie translated Qin in the early 19th century is wrong on its own evidence: Wylie lived 1815-1887 and his Jottings on the Science of the Chinese was published in 1853 (Shanghai); the Sunzi date remains a range, MacTutor listing 3rd to 5th century opinions, c.400-460 for the author, and one scholar's 237 AD.
source: Wikipedia, Alexander Wylie (missionary); MacTutor, Sun Zi
note: Read Wikipedia CRT, Wylie and MacTutor Sun Zi pages; the coinage of the name 'Chinese remainder theorem' was not found (Crossref title search gave nothing), so that part is still unresolved.

fact: The 1575 printing of Maurolico's Arithmeticorum libri duo (written 1557) is confirmed by Wikipedia and MacTutor, but 'first induction proof' is contested: Wikipedia credits Gersonides (1288-1344) with the earliest rigorous use and al-Karaji c.1000 with an implicit one, so the label 'first' should be softened to 'early printed explicit use'.
note: Read Wikipedia Mathematical induction and the MacTutor Maurolico page; year confirmed, priority claim not supported.

fact: Wikipedia dates De prospectiva pingendi to the mid-1470s (possibly about 1474, probably between 1474 and 1482), not the 1460s.
note: Read Wikipedia's article on the treatise and MacTutor Mathematics and art; the 1460s option is not supported there; the milestone year 1470 is inside no source range and should read c.1474-1482.

fact: Leibniz's Nova methodus pro maximis et minimis appeared in Acta Eruditorum in October 1684 and is the first published calculus work; Newton's manuscripts (1665-66) are unpublished, so they are precursors.
source: Wikipedia, Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis; Lemley 2021, The Library 22(2)
note: Searched Wikipedia and Crossref, which holds Lemley's study dating the October 1684 printing; naming of 'calculus' was not searched here.

fact: Newton's tract De motu corporum in gyrum was sent to Halley in November 1684, and Principia opens with a revised version of it; the title is confirmed by Wikipedia's Principia article.
note: Read the Wikipedia Principia article and MacTutor Newton (which also mentions the 1684 tract); the Hooke and Leibniz priority questions were not addressed.

fact: Dirichlet introduced the characters (and L-functions) in his 1837 paper on primes in arithmetic progressions, per Wikipedia, and Wikipedia says the characters were named after him; the date or author of the phrases 'Dirichlet character' and 'analytic number theory' was not found.
note: Read Wikipedia's Dirichlet character and Analytic number theory pages and a Crossref search for the 1837 paper (only reprints indexed); no coinage date appeared.

fact: Wikipedia credits the principle of duality to Gergonne (with Brianchon on plane duality), not Poncelet alone; von Staudt's rigorous Geometrie der Lage is dated 1847, which can be added as a dated milestone.
source: Wikipedia, Duality (projective geometry); Wikipedia, Karl von Staudt
note: Read both Wikipedia pages and MacTutor Poncelet; Desargues' root remains undated in what I read.

fact: Crossref lists Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson, Solution of Kirkman's schoolgirl problem, in Proc. Symp. Pure Math. 19 (1971); Wikipedia adds that Lu Jiaxi proved it in 1965 but was unpublished, and dates the Ray-Chaudhuri-Wilson proof to 1968.
note: Checked Crossref and Wikipedia's Kirkman page; publication year 1971 confirmed, the priority question is as the record states (Lu earlier, unpublished).

fact: Hoüel's French translation of Beltrami's Saggio appeared in Annales scientifiques de l'ENS, Series 1, vol. 6 (1869), pp. 251-288, not 1870; the companion translation of the Teoria fondamentale is also 1869 (doi 10.24033/asens.62).
note: Found the translation record on Numdam and Crossref; MacTutor's 1870 date is therefore off by one for these two translations.

fact: Crossref lists a paper titled 'A Galois theory for differential fields' (Duke Math. J., 1943, doi 10.1215/s0012-7094-43-01071-3), so the phrase predates Kolchin's 1953 'Galois Theory of Differential Fields' (Am. J. Math. 75, doi 10.2307/2372550); it is the earliest title use found, not a verified coinage.
note: Crossref title searches for 'Galois theory of differential fields' and 'Picard-Vessiot theory' up to 1965; the author listed is Eaton (not Ritt), and no earlier title was found, but Ritt's books were not searched.

fact: The Stanford Encyclopedia says the 1900 problem was followed by a sketch of a consistency proof in the Heidelberg talk (1905), and that Hilbert's own proposal was presented in three Hamburg talks of summer 1921 (published 1922); Wikipedia dates the programme to the early 1920s, so the 1905 lecture is better classed as a precursor and the first_statement as 1922.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Hilbert's Program; Wikipedia, Hilbert's program
note: Read the SEP entry and Wikipedia page; the lecture text itself was not read, so 1905 as precursor rests on the two secondary accounts.

fact: zbMATH lists Julia, 'Sur les substitutions rationnelles', C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 165 (1917) 1098-1100, and Fatou's note of the same title in C. R. 164 (1917) 806-808, so the venue is the Comptes rendus and both notes are 1917.
note: Queried the zbMATH Open API for Julia and Fatou 1917; found both notes with series C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris.

fact: Wikipedia says Fisher's 1921 paper introduced what is now the likelihood interval while the 1922 foundations paper (Crossref 10.1098/rsta.1922.0009, Phil. Trans. A 222) proposed the term likelihood and maximum likelihood, and MacTutor agrees with 1921 for the concept; so the concept dates to 1921 and the 1922 paper is the naming and full statement.
note: Checked Crossref for the 1922 paper (found) and the 1921 Metron paper (not indexed there); the conflict is thus partly a naming-versus-concept difference.

fact: Crossref records Kolmogoroff, 'Uber die analytischen Methoden in der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung', Mathematische Annalen, issue of December 1931, so MacTutor's 1938 is not supported; the Bachelier 1900 precursor is also confirmed by Crossref (Ann. Sci. ENS, doi 10.24033/asens.476).
note: Crossref title searches for both papers returned records with 1931 and 1900 as issue years.

fact: Crossref gives Shannon, 'Communication in the Presence of Noise', Proc. IRE 37, pp. 10-21 (January 1949), and Wikipedia says Shannon stated and proved the sampling theorem in it, so the claim that it develops the theory is supported at least for the sampling theorem.
note: Checked Crossref for the record and Wikipedia for content; the paper text itself was not read, so other content (geometric signal space) is not verified.

fact: Open Library lists two separate Atiyah 'K-theory' editions, 1964 (the Harvard lecture-notes edition) and 1967 (Benjamin book), so the conflict is two different publications: the notes are the earlier systematic treatment (1964) and the Benjamin book is 1967.
note: Queried the Open Library search API for title K-theory and author Atiyah; found 1964 and 1967 works; the Borel-Serre 1958 and Atiyah-Hirzebruch 1959 years were not in dispute.

fact: zbMATH shows Unterberger and Bokobza had a C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris note in 1964 (vol. 259, 1612-1614, 'Les operateurs de Calderon-Zygmund precises') but its title does not use the term; the first title using 'pseudo-differentiels' by them is C. R. 261 (1965), 2271-2273, after the Kohn-Nirenberg paper in Commun. Pure Appl. Math. 18 (1965), 269-305, so the 1965 date and title priority for the name stand while the 1964 French note is an earlier related result.
note: Queried zbMATH for Unterberger, Bokobza and Kohn-Nirenberg 1963-1966; ordering of the two 1965 items rests on volume numbers (CPAM 18 early 1965, C. R. 261 second half of 1965), not on exact dates.

fact: Buchi's decision-method paper appeared in the proceedings of the 1960 Congress published in 1962 (pp. 1-11, per a Journal of Symbolic Logic review in Crossref), and his earlier automata-logic paper, Weak second-order arithmetic and finite automata, is Z. Math. Logik 6 (1960); the scope question (event title versus Floyd-Hoare summary) is an editorial choice, not a factual one.
note: Checked Crossref and Wikipedia Buchi automaton for the precursor dates; other years in the record (Floyd 1967, Hoare 1969, Pnueli 1977) were seen only in the record, and the scope dispute has no external source.

fact: Crossref gives Yau's announcement, Calabi's conjecture and some new results in algebraic geometry, PNAS 74(5), 1798-1799 (May 1977), and the full proof appeared in Commun. Pure Appl. Math. 31 (1978); MacTutor says only that Yau solved it in 1976, so the two dates are compatible (solution 1976, publication 1977-78) and the record's publication-year rule is sound.
note: Checked Crossref for the PNAS issue date and MacTutor and Wikipedia for the 1976 claim; the coinage of 'Calabi-Yau' was not searched.

fact: Sato's 'Soliton equations as dynamical systems on an infinite dimensional Grassmann manifolds' appeared in RIMS Kokyuroku 439 (1981), pp. 30-46, from a Kyoto symposium of 7-9 January 1981, so it predates the 1983 North-Holland version; the 1981 first statement can replace 1983.
source: zbMATH Open 3800630 (Zbl 0507.58029) and RIMS Kokyuroku No. 439 contents page
note: Queried zbMATH for Sato 1980-1984 and opened the RIMS Kokyuroku 439 table of contents, which lists the paper at page 30 with the symposium dates in January 1981.

fact: zbMATH lists Mordell, 'On the rational solutions of the indeterminate equations of the third and fourth degrees', Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 21 (1922), 179-192, the paper where the Mordell conjecture is stated.
note: Crossref title search found nothing, zbMATH author and year search found the record; that the conjecture is stated in this paper is from Wikipedia and MacTutor, not re-read.

fact: MacTutor dates the Bhagabati Sutra to about 300 BC and the Sthananga Sutra to about the 2nd century BC, and Wikipedia gives Pingala as c. 3rd or 2nd century BCE; the ranges overlap and no source read gives an order, so the relative order stays open.
note: Read both pages; the Kusuba-Plofker chapter cited in the record was not opened, so a firmer chronology may exist there.

fact: Wikipedia's Algorism and MacTutor say only that al-Khwarizmi's Hindu-numeral treatise was translated into Latin in the 12th century as Algoritmi de numero Indorum (Arabic text lost); no exact year is given, so the 1100 date is the start of a century range, not a dated event. Wikipedia adds first English use about 1230 and the verse Carmen de Algorismo about 1240.
note: Read Wikipedia Algorism, Al-Khwarizmi and MacTutor Al-Khwarizmi; no translator or year was stated, so the naming milestone should carry a range 1100-1199, not 1100.

fact: No source I could open dates Tusi's Treatise on the Quadrilateral: MacTutor and Wikipedia only call it the first extant exposition of the whole system of plane and spherical trigonometry and independent of astronomy, and MacTutor gives the Maragheh observatory as operational in 1262; Encyclopaedia Iranica and Britannica pages returned nothing.
note: Read MacTutor and Wikipedia on Tusi, Wikipedia History of trigonometry, Open Library, and tried Iranica and Britannica; the al-Jayyani priority was not settled; Van Brummelen's book was not accessible.

fact: Viete's answer to van Roomen's degree-45 problem is dated 1595 by MacTutor, but I could not find a dated record of the posthumous Ad angulares sectiones; Internet Archive holds the 1615 De aequationum recognitione (ita-bnc-mag-00000885-001, edited by Alexander Anderson) and Schooten's 1646 Opera mathematica (bub_gb_25iHrtJpy9oC), whose OCR mentions angular sections but gives no usable date.
source: MacTutor, Francois Viete; Internet Archive Schooten 1646
note: Searched MacTutor, Wikipedia (no mention), Open Library, zbMATH and the Internet Archive text of Schooten's Opera; no bibliographic record for the title was found.

fact: Wikipedia credits Graunt with the first life table and treats Petty as a collaborator, with the book presented to the Royal Society on 5 February 1661 (probably Old Style, so 1662); the Graunt versus Petty authorship question and the first use of the term 'life table' were not settled by anything I could open.
note: Read Wikipedia John Graunt and Life table; found no authorship ruling or coinage date; the ODNB and a Graunt edition were not accessible.

fact: Wikipedia says the formula is named after de Moivre although he never stated it, and cites Braunmuhl 1901 (Bibliotheca Mathematica, 3rd series 2, 97-102) on the 'so-called Moivre theorem', so the name existed by 1901, but its coinage is not dated; Crossref confirms De sectione anguli in Phil. Trans. vol. 32 (1722) and the 1707 and 1711 papers.
note: Checked Crossref for the three Philosophical Transactions DOIs (all match their years) and Wikipedia for the name; an earlier use of the phrase was not found.

fact: Wikipedia's Laplace's equation article says Laplace first studied the equation in 1786, not 1782, and Newton's potential article credits Newton with the Newtonian potential; I could not open any source on Lagrange's 1773 memoir on attraction, so the first use of the potential function remains unsettled between Lagrange (c.1773) and Laplace (1782-86).
note: Read Wikipedia Laplace's equation, Newtonian potential and Lagrange, and MacTutor Lagrange; none dates Lagrange's attraction memoir, and the zbMATH query for it returned nothing.

fact: The Internet Archive scan of the second edition of Dirichlet-Dedekind Vorlesungen uber Zahlentheorie (Vieweg, Braunschweig, 1871; preface dated 1 March 1871) contains Supplement X with a general theory of ideals (section 163), so the 1871 date is verified and MacTutor's 1879 and 1894 refer to later editions.
source: Internet Archive, Vorlesungen uber Zahlentheorie, 2nd edition (1871)
note: Searched archive.org, downloaded the OCR text of the 1871 item and read the title page, preface and table of contents; the preface states the supplement includes a general theory of ideals.

fact: Wikipedia quotes Hilbert's 1900 problem text as crediting L. Schlesinger (1895) with a proof in the unit-modulus case via Poincare's Fuchsian zeta-functions; zbMATH lists Schlesinger's Handbuch der Theorie der linearen Differentialgleichungen vol. I (1895), vol. II part 1 (1897) and part 2 (1898), and Plemelj's 1909 note (Jahresber. DMV 18) questions Schlesinger's 'proof', but no source names the exact 1895 work.
source: zbMATH Open 2637289 (Plemelj 1909); Wikipedia, Hilbert's twenty-first problem
note: Queried zbMATH for Schlesinger 1894-1899 and Handbuch, and read Wikipedia's problem article; the proof is not tied to a titled paper, so the year 1895 is Hilbert's own citation and the title stays unidentified.

fact: zbMATH lists Poincare, 'Sur les fonctions fuchsiennes', C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris 92 (1881), pp. 333-336, plus further 1881 notes in the same journal and Math. Ann. 19 (1881), 553-565, so the individual 1881 notes are now located.
note: Queried zbMATH for Poincare 1881; Crossref was not needed.

fact: Hilbert's basis theorem is in 'Uber die Theorie der algebraischen Formen', Math. Ann. 36 (1890), 473-534 (Crossref, Wikipedia), while the 1893 Math. Ann. 42 paper is 'Uber die vollen Invariantensysteme'; so 1890 is the basis theorem and MacTutor's 1893 refers to the second paper. Macaulay's 1915 uniqueness result stays unchecked.
note: Searched Crossref for both Hilbert papers and read Wikipedia's basis theorem page; did not search Macaulay or the coinage of 'ring'.

fact: zbMATH lists Reidemeister's Knotentheorie as Ergebnisse der Mathematik 1 (1932), a dedicated monograph, and his earlier group-theoretic paper Knoten und Gruppen is dated 1926 by Wikipedia; the book's content was not read, so the consolidation role is plausible but unverified.
note: Queried zbMATH and read Wikipedia and MacTutor on Reidemeister; year and series confirmed, content not opened.

fact: zbMATH lists Chang and Keisler, Model theory, Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics 73 (1973), so the two-author citation is verified.
note: Open Library gave no 1973 edition in search; zbMATH returned the record with both authors; the 'model theory' naming was not searched.

fact: Crossref records 'Beweis eines Hauptsatzes in der Theorie der Algebren' by Brauer, Hasse and Noether, J. reine angew. Math. 167 (1932), 399-404, confirming the joint authorship; the naming of noncommutative algebra as a field remains undated.
note: Crossref title search up to 1935; no search was run for a field name.

fact: Crossref and zbMATH list Magnus, 'A connection between the Baker-Hausdorff formula and a problem of Burnside', Ann. of Math. (2) 52 (1950), 111-126 (July 1950); the title does not contain the phrase 'restricted Burnside problem', so whether it coined that name was not checked.
note: Found the record in both indices; the year is verified, the naming role is not.

fact: Crossref confirms Hirzebruch's PNAS 40(2), February 1954, 'Arithmetic genera and the theorem of Riemann-Roch for algebraic varieties' (doi 10.1073/pnas.40.2.110); no source found dates the coinage of the name 'Hirzebruch-Riemann-Roch', which the Wikipedia article uses without history.
note: Checked Crossref and the Wikipedia article for the name; no earlier use or coinage found.

fact: Crossref and zbMATH list Kodaira's Complex Manifolds and Deformation of Complex Structures as Grundlehren 283 (Springer, 1986), translated from the Japanese by Kazuo Akao, with a Classics in Mathematics reprint in 2005 (not 2006).
note: Queried Crossref and zbMATH; the Japanese original year was not checked.

fact: arXiv shows Jin, Milojevic, Tomon and Zhang posted 3 September 2025 (abstract calls its bound the first polynomial bound for Chowla's cosine problem, 1965), two days before Bedert's 5 September 2025 preprint; the abstract does not mention clique-free Cayley graphs, so that wording stays unverified, and Chowla's 1965 paper was not located.
note: Queried the arXiv API for both preprints; 'first' is the authors' claim, but the posting dates support it among these two.

fact: zbMATH lists Levin, 'Universal problems of full search', Probl. Peredachi Inf. 9 (1973), 115-116; Wikipedia says the term NP-complete was introduced later and popularised by Aho, Hopcroft and Ullman per Knuth, so no naming year is established.
note: Crossref found nothing for Levin; zbMATH found the record; the Knuth 1974 terminological proposal was seen only as a Wikipedia reference.

Math. 31 (1979), where Wikipedia says the first case of the fundamental lemma (SL2) was considered; zbMATH dates Langlands' 'Les debuts d'une formule des traces stable' to 1982 while Wikipedia says 1983, so the 1983 conjecture date is uncertain by a year.
